name: Reattachment rhinoplasty

card.summary: A family of nose-reshaping techniques in which cartilage or bone that is reduced is put back in place rather than discarded, used to lower a dorsal hump while keeping a natural, smooth bridge line.
card.aka: nasal reattachment; recycled hump; Skoog-type dorsal reduction
card.note: Surgical procedure with revision risk; outcomes data come mostly from surgeon-authored case series.

quick.overview:
Reattachment rhinoplasty refers to approaches where the cartilage (and sometimes bone) of the nasal dorsum is cut free, reduced and then repositioned or sutured back, instead of being simply shaved off. The aesthetic goal is a lower or straighter bridge that still has smooth, natural-looking dorsal lines and a stable middle third of the nose.

Surgeons who use it describe it as a way to reduce a hump while preserving the structures that support the middle vault of the nose. Evidence consists of case series from individual surgeons, such as a 22-patient series published in 2003; no randomized comparisons with conventional hump removal are listed here.
quick.how: It is performed by a facial plastic or ENT surgeon, typically through an open approach under anesthesia. The upper lateral cartilages are freed, the hump segment is removed or lowered, trimmed to fit, and then sutured back so the bridge sits flat on the midline. Surgeons usually reserve the technique for humps that are mostly cartilaginous. Swelling takes months to settle.
quick.risks: As with any rhinoplasty, risks include bleeding, hematoma, asymmetry, irregularities of the bridge, breathing problems and the need for revision. In published series some patients needed a second operation for a residual hump or a visible ridge. Surgeons caution that the technique is not suited to every nose, for example primarily bony humps.

lead: Reattachment rhinoplasty is an informal name used in looksmaxxing circles for nose surgery in which tissue removed from the nasal dorsum is replaced instead of discarded. The best-documented example in the surgical literature is the 'Skoog' type of dorsal reduction, where the cartilaginous hump is resected as a segment, trimmed and sewn back to the surrounding cartilage. [2]

People pursue it to lower a dorsal hump while keeping a smooth, straight bridge and supporting the middle third of the nose, which can otherwise narrow or collapse after conventional reduction. [2] Reduction rhinoplasty itself has a long history, with Jacques Joseph describing refined internal-incision methods in 1928, and reconstruction by reattaching tissue goes back to Tagliacozzi in 1597. [1]

Published evidence is limited to surgeon-reported case series and technique descriptions. Related dorsum-preserving approaches, such as push-down techniques, have also been described, with reports of both good dorsal lines and a risk of recurrence of the hump. [3]

chain: Hump segment is lowered and trimmed
Segment is sutured back into place
Smooth, lower bridge with a supported middle third
angle.text: The procedure reduces a dorsal hump and aims to leave natural dorsal aesthetic lines and a stable middle vault. People choose it for a straighter profile and for a bridge that looks less operated-on.

paras: In conventional hump reduction the cartilage portion is cut with a scalpel and the bony part chiseled and rasped smooth. [1] Reattachment-style methods instead keep the removed dorsal segment. In the modification of the Skoog technique reported by Hall, Peters and Hilger, the upper lateral cartilages are freed from the septum and nasal bones, the bony-cartilaginous dorsum is taken out as one segment, the underlying septal remnant is trimmed so the segment lies flat and midline, and the upper lateral cartilages are then sutured to its edges. [2]
The segment is repeatedly replaced and the soft tissue redraped during the operation to avoid over-reduction. [2]

The authors described using it for primarily cartilaginous humps in patients at risk of middle vault collapse, such as those with short nasal bones, flaccid upper lateral cartilages or thin dorsal skin, with limited deviation and a base that did not need osteotomies. They did not use it for primarily bony humps. [2]

Reattachment of tissue in nasal surgery is old: in 1597 Gasparo Tagliacozzi illustrated reconstructing a nose with a flap from the upper arm. [1] Modern reduction rhinoplasty developed through Jacques Joseph's 1928 work, the endonasal approach of John Orlando Roe (1887) and the open approach introduced in the 1930s and popularized in the 1970s. [1] The Skoog dorsal reduction and later modifications aim to retain, rather than discard, the dorsal roof.

In the 2003 series of 22 patients with at least 9 months of follow-up, the authors reported adequate dorsal reduction, preserved middle vault width and natural dorsal lines; one patient developed a visible lateral ridge and was revised, and none had internal valve collapse, though airway assessment was subjective. [2]

A different dorsum-preserving series from Brazil (153 patients, 2011-2015) reported a low complication rate, with 13 patients needing a second operation for a residual hump. [3] Reviews cited in the literature note that dorsum-preserving techniques can give pleasing dorsal lines but may have a higher rate of hump recurrence. [3]

Published work consists of retrospective case series from individual surgeons, including the 22-patient 2003 series on the modified Skoog technique and a 153-patient series on a related push-down technique. [2][3] Neither compared the technique with conventional reduction in a randomized trial.

timeline.event: Tagliacozzi illustrates a reattachment-style nasal reconstruction with an arm flap. [1]
Roe performs the first modern endonasal rhinoplasty. [1]
Joseph publishes refined internal-incision nose reduction methods. [1]
Hall, Peters and Hilger publish a modification of the Skoog dorsal reduction. [2]
